With sixty children in Class 6C and the half-yearly exam two weeks away, Mr Iyer moved fast. On the first day of term he had said, "Sachin, maths is not your subject, na?" and everyone had laughed.
Now, when a question came, his eyes went straight past Sachin to Siddharth and the front benches. If Sachin did raise his hand, Mr Iyer counted one second, then said, "Anyone else?" So Sachin stopped raising it. He drew cricket bats in the margin and waited for the bell.
On the test he left the word problems blank without reading them. "I'm weak at maths," he told Siddharth, as if it were his name. Siddharth said, "You solved my sums for me yesterday, though."

qa.q: How many children are in Class 6C?
qa.a: Sixty children.

qa.q: What was Sachin feeling when he left the word problems blank?
qa.a: He felt discouraged and resigned, believing the label so much that he didn't even try.

qa.q: What could Mr Iyer change, even with sixty students and little time?
qa.a: Wait a few seconds for every raised hand, including Sachin's, and stop saying maths is "not your subject".

qa.q: How does Siddharth see Sachin's maths?
qa.a: Siddharth knows Sachin solved his sums yesterday, so he sees ability that the label hides.

grounding: Shows a child labelled weak at maths getting less waiting time and fewer questions, giving up raising his hand, until the label seems true.

At the tuition centre above the sweet shop in Pune, Neelam ma'am divided the class into "fast" and "slow" rows on the first day. Nilesh went to the slow row because he had made two mistakes in the entrance quiz.
After that, the fast row got the puzzles and the slow row got worksheets. When Nilesh asked a question, ma'am answered quickly without looking up. When the fast row asked, she pulled up a chair.
By October Nilesh had stopped asking. He copied answers from the back of the book and told his mother, "I'm in the slow row. Maths isn't for me." The word "slow" had settled on him like dust.

qa.q: Why was Nilesh put in the slow row?
qa.a: Because he had made two mistakes in the entrance quiz.

qa.q: What was Nilesh feeling when he told his mother "Maths isn't for me"?
qa.a: He felt defeated and small, having absorbed the "slow" label until it felt like the truth about him.

qa.q: What went wrong at the tuition centre, and what could fix it?
qa.a: One quiz decided who got puzzles and attention; mixing the rows and giving everyone puzzles and full answers would help.

qa.q: How might the fast-row children see Nilesh?
qa.a: They may assume he really is slow, since they never see him get puzzles or long explanations.

grounding: Shows a child placed in a 'slow' group receiving fewer challenges and less attention, then giving up asking until the label becomes his belief.

In their village near Dharwad, Bhavna's grandmother had a line she said at every festival: "This one will never be like her cousin Latha." Latha was a nurse in Bengaluru now. Bhavna was the one who had failed Kannada in ninth.
By sixteen, Bhavna said it herself before anyone else could: "I'm not the clever one." She stopped going to evening tuition and sat at the family's kirana shop instead.
Her mother, Sharmila, watched this for a year. Then, one quiet afternoon, she handed Bhavna the shop's accounts book. "You count faster than me. Do this week's totals." Bhavna frowned but did them, twice to be sure. Every total matched. Sharmila said nothing, only handed her next week's book too.

qa.q: Where is Latha a nurse now?
qa.a: In Bengaluru.

qa.a: She feels ashamed and resigned, and saying it first protects her from the sting of hearing it again.

qa.q: Why might Sharmila's quiet trust help more than a speech?
qa.a: Giving Bhavna real work she can do well shows belief through action, letting Bhavna see her own ability.

qa.q: How might Bhavna's grandmother see her if she watched her do the accounts?
qa.a: She might be surprised to see a capable girl instead of the less clever cousin she keeps describing.

grounding: Shows a teenager adopting a family verdict about never matching her cousin as her identity, and a parent's quiet trust starting to lift her.
